subject: Banking
title: Underwriting IPOs and Bonds
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Underwriting IPOs and Bonds.

hook.text: When a company goes public, investment banks charge 3-7% of the total raised.

buildup.text: Underwriting means the bank buys all the shares first, then resells them to investors. The bank guarantees the sale.

discovery.text: Banks also underwrite bond issuances. Governments and corporations pay fees to have banks distribute their debt.

twist.text: Banks sometimes underprice IPOs deliberately. The 'pop' on day one makes their clients happy and brings more deal flow.

climax.text: Underwriting is risk for hire. Banks get paid to absorb the uncertainty of selling new securities to the market.

punchline.text: Up to 7% of billions raised. IPO underwriting is high-stakes fee income.

quiz.question: What percentage do banks typically charge for underwriting an IPO?

details.summary: Banks earn billions underwriting initial public offerings and bond issuances, charging fees of 2 to 7 percent for managing the complex process of bringing new securities to market and distributing them to investors.
details.whyItMatters: Underwriting is how companies raise capital from public markets, and bank fees directly affect the cost of financing. The concentrated market power of a few banks influences how efficiently capital flows through the economy.
takeaways: IPO underwriting fees typically range from 5 to 7 percent of proceeds
Bond underwriting fees are lower, usually 0.5 to 1.5 percent
The top 10 investment banks handle over 70 percent of global underwriting

faq.question: Why are IPO underwriting fees so high?
faq.answer: Banks argue the fee covers extensive due diligence, roadshow costs, regulatory compliance, and the risk of committing to buy shares they might not sell. Critics note that fees have remained at 7% for decades despite technology reducing costs significantly.

faq.question: How do banks choose the IPO price?
faq.answer: Underwriters gauge investor demand through a bookbuilding process, collecting non-binding purchase commitments at various prices. Banks face a conflict of interest: underpricing pleases their investor clients while overpricing pleases the issuing company.
